In brief

Episode 13, "Nausicaa," takes place between 8 and 9 PM in a spot on the Sandymount Strand that Stephen Dedalus walked past in Proteus—yet another non-meeting of the protagonists. Bloom has come to this place for reasons that are not immediately apparent, and his identity is not revealed until more than half the chapter has elapsed. Until that point, strange new kinds of prose narrative suggestive of female sensibility describe three young women, a baby, and two small boys as they enjoy an evening on the beach not far from Bloom. One of the women is drawn to him, and he to her, by erotic gazing that produces romantic rapture in her and a more notably carnal effect in him—effects echoed in the fireworks going off above the nearby Mirus Bazaar. Joyce had written of erotic seaside gazes before, but when he composed this scene he found a new model in Homer's story of Odysseus encountering a young woman on a beach. The chapter's outrageous sexual content got Ulysses banned in the UK and the US, but its juxtaposition of incompatible imaginative perspectives is even more daring. Recasting Odysseus's heroic adventure as a girl's romantic love story is wildly inventive, and in the second half of the chapter Joyce takes the wind out of both sails by showing Bloom's thoughts to be neither heroic nor romantic. Here he is merely a melancholic, weary masturbator.

At more length

Book 5 of Homer's poem tells how Odysseus, who has gained his release from Calypso's island, sails for many days and then is shipwrecked by Poseidon. After floating desperately for a long time, clinging to a beam—echoed in the chapter when Bloom thinks of shipwrecked sailors "Hanging on to a plank or astride of a beam for grim life"—he washes up on an unknown beach battered, exhausted, and naked, crawls under some bushes, and falls asleep. Book 6 tells how, the next morning, the lovely young princess of the Phaeacians who rule this island drives a wagon loaded with clothes down to the water to wash them, because she hopes to find a husband and must look her best. She and her slaves do the laundry, bathe, rub oil into their bodies, eat, and then throw a ball to each other. Nausicaa is good at the play, but one of her companions fails to catch the ball, which rolls into an eddy. Odysseus is waked by the sound of women shrieking. He emerges naked, covered only with a leafy branch, to the terror of the slave girls, but Nausicaa stands her ground.

He wondered, should he touch her knees, or keep
some distance and use charming words, to beg
the pretty girl to show him to the town,
and give him clothes. At last he thought it best
to keep some distance and use words to beg her.
The girl might be alarmed at being touched.
His words were calculated flattery.
                                     (6.142-48, trans. Wilson)

Addressing the young woman as if she might be a goddess, he says, "that man will be luckiest by far, / who takes you home with dowry, as his bride. / I have seen no one like you. Never, no one. My eyes are dazzled when I look at you" (158-61). Relating his ordeal, he begs her to give him some clothes and show him the way to town: "So may the gods grant all your heart's desires, / a home and husband, somebody like-minded" (181-81). Nausicaa agrees, and after Odysseus washes the salt from his hair and rubs his skin with oil, Athena makes him too appear godlike: "his handsomeness was dazzling. The girl was shocked.... Before, he looked so poor and unrefined; / now he is like a god that lives in heaven. I hope I get a man like this as husband" (238-39, 243-45). She tells him how to get to her father's house but declines to accompany him, because people would talk: "So they will shame me. I myself would blame / a girl who got too intimate with men / before her marriage" (284-86).

Joyce mimics every major element of this scene. Like Nausicaa, Gerty MacDowell is lovely: "as fair a specimen of winsome Irish girlhood as one could wish to see," with a mouth that is "Greekly perfect," and "an innate refinement, a languid queenly hauteur." She dresses herself in fine clothes because the young man whom she hopes to marry may see her in them: "Gerty was dressed simply but with the instinctive taste of a votary of Dame Fashion for she felt that there was just a might that he might be out." But she dreams also that an older man might take an interest in her, "a manly man with a strong quiet face who had not found his ideal, perhaps his hair slightly flecked with grey... For such a one she yearns this balmy summer eve. With all the heart of her she longs to be his only, his affianced bride."

Gerty goes to the seaside with some female companions to whom she feels superior, not to wash clothes as Nausicaa does but to babysit three children. The two twin boys play with a ball, one of them kicks it hard, and it finds its way down to the seaweedy rocks where Bloom sits: "luckily the gentleman in black who was sitting there by himself came gallantly to the rescue and intercepted the ball." He throws it back, inaccurately, and it lands at the feet of Gerty, who (less athletic than Nausicaa, for reasons revealed later) attempts to kick it back to the boys but misses. This mutually inept interaction draws her attention to the man, and his sad face moves her. Sounds waft out of the Star of the Sea church, imploring the protectress of sailors. Gerty sees the man gazing at her and is aroused: "Wonderful eyes they were, superbly expressive, but could you trust them? People were so queer. She could see at once by his dark eyes and his pale intellectual face that he was a foreigner, the image of the photo she had of Martin Harvey, the matinee idol." All of these details—the rolling ball, a solitary unhappy man by the seashore, his foreignness, the uncertainty whether to trust him, the godlike handsomeness of his face—clearly reenact the events of the Odyssey.

Somewhat less obvious, but even more delightful, is the way Joyce recasts Homer's scene of a naive young woman meeting a more experienced older man. Nausicaa thinks she may have found a husband, but Odysseus is only using "calculated flattery" to effect a rescue. Similarly, Gerty decides that Bloom is her "dreamhusband" and quickly spins fantasies of a married life with him, but Bloom takes advantage of her romantic transport to gratify needs more immediate and less troublesome than matrimony. Nausicaa is attracted to the stranger but wary of what people may think. Gerty more brazenly skirts the limits of maiden modesty, allowing Bloom to feast his eyes on her and even leaning back to show him her underwear, but she does not want to be thought immoral and absolves herself of any sexual desire. It is Bloom, "eying her as a snake eyes its prey," who performs the immoral action, somewhat like the lodger than Bertha Supple has told her about "that had pictures cut out of papers of those skirtdancers and highkickers and she said he used to do something not very nice that you could imagine sometimes in the bed. But this was altogether different from a thing like that."

Homer's bold idea of introducing a naked man into a group of young women, his penis concealed by a branch, inspires Joyce to even bolder imitation. When Cissy goes over to Bloom to ask him for the time, "she could see him take his hand out of his pocket, getting nervous." Gerty sees him as "a man of inflexible honour to his fingertips. His hands and face were working." This hilarious allusion may make one think of the moment, reported in Richard Ellmann's biography, when a young admirer approached Joyce in a Zurich café to ask, "May I kiss the hand that wrote Ulysses?" "No," replied Joyce, "it did lots of other things too" (110).

Joyce critics seldom remark on how extensively Nausicaa echoes Homer's action, probably because the echoes of different literary models tend to drown it out. By the technique of free indirect narration used elsewhere to foreground the sensibilities of Stephen, Bloom, and some other characters, more than half of this chapter hovers close to Gerty's thoughts, parodying the style of things that a woman like her would read. Romance novels of the 19th century privileged feeling over thought, making a virtue of sentimentality, and advertisements endlessly pitched beauty products. Joyce's prose here, an extension of the parodic principle introduced in Cyclops, is a master class in cloying sentimentality, preciosity, cliché, confessional intimacy, and beauty tips. In a 1920 letter to his friend Frank Budgen, Joyce said that it is "written in a namby-pamby jammy marmalady drawersy (alto là!) style with effects of incense, mariolatry, masturbation, stewed cockles, painter's palette, chitchat, circumlocutions, etc., etc."

One woman's novel, Maria Cummins's The Lamplighter, is famously a source, though its prose style does not greatly resemble Nausicaa's. Cummins's book contributes some plot elements to the ones acquired from the Odyssey. Her heroine, Gerty Flint, is imperfect but pious. Finding religion and learning self-control, she is rewarded with marriage to her childhood sweetheart Willie (his name resembles Joyce's Reggy Wylie) and rises from poverty to wealth. These motifs clearly contribute to the dream life of Joyce's character, but they do not figure much in the chapter's action. Gerty MacDowell's complicity in the lustful fantasy of a stranger comes instead from Homer, whose hero is a married man trying to get back to his wife but who is not averse to some opportune flirtation. Instead of an introduction to the king of Scheria, Bloom gains some relief from his present defeated condition: "Goodbye, dear. Thanks. Made me feel so young."

As for the question of why he is on this beach in the first place, that is slowly answered as the chapter proceeds. At several points Gerty mentions "Mr Dignam and Mrs and Patsy and Freddy Dignam," whose Sandymount house is quite nearby, and Bloom later thinks of "coming out of Dignam's." Still later he thinks, "Off colour after Kiernan's, Dignam's. For this relief much thanks." Cyclops showed him going to Barney Kiernan's pub to meet Martin Cunningham about the collection for Dignam's widow, and now it becomes clear that they have paid her a visit. Confrontations with a violent nationalist in a dark pub and a grieving widow in a house of mourning have left him "Off colour," and sexual satisfaction goes a long way toward restoring his peace of mind.

Cyclops ends at about 6 PM and Nausicaa begins at about 8. Although some distance separates the pub near Capel Street and the house in Sandymount, traversing it would take nothing like two hours. Much of this time must have been spent in the Dignams' house, but Joyce chooses not to represent the scene. In a novel structured around successive hours of one day, why might he have chosen to leave this two-hour gap unfilled? Various explanations seem possible, but Don Gifford's may be the best: true acts of charity do not call attention to themselves. According to Matthew 6:3, the right hand should not know what the left is doing. Bloom does not come off altogether well from the narration in Nausicaa, but an action that is not narrated goes some way toward balancing the account.

John Hunt 2025
